text.en: Raju saw paddy fields on the way to his village. "What do farmers grow here?" he asked.

Agriculture is the main occupation in Tamil Nadu. Rice is the chief food crop, and other crops include millets, pulses, sugarcane, cotton, groundnut and coconut. Nutmeg, tea and coffee are grown in the hills.
Water comes from rivers like the Cauvery, from tanks, canals and wells, and the delta region is the rice bowl. Farming depends on monsoon rain, and the Kuruvai, Samba and Thaladi seasons are known in Tamil Nadu.
Farmers face problems such as erratic rain, low prices and debt. Modern methods, drip irrigation, crop insurance and organic farming help, and the Green Revolution raised yields.

Farming depends on monsoon rain, and the Kuruvai, Samba and Thaladi seasons are known in Tamil Nadu.
Farmers face problems such as erratic rain, low prices and debt.
Modern methods, drip irrigation, crop insurance and organic farming help, and the Green Revolution raised yields.
Let us look closely at how Tamil Nadu's land is used. Roughly half of the state's geographical area is put to farming or related rural use, while forests, towns and fallow lands share the rest.
Most farmers in Tamil Nadu are small and marginal cultivators who own less than two hectares of land. Because plots are small, family labour plays a huge role in sowing, weeding and harvesting.
Tamil Nadu receives most of its rain from the Northeast Monsoon between October and December, unlike much of northern India which relies mainly on the Southwest Monsoon.
Because Tamil Nadu has no perennial snow-fed river, farmers store seasonal rain in three main ways: canals, tanks and wells.
Canal irrigation is strongest in the Cauvery delta districts such as Thanjavur, Tiruvarur and Nagapattinam, where channels branch from the Mettur Dam and Grand Anicut.
Ancient eris and tanks built by Chola and Pandya rulers still recharge groundwater and supply fields across southern and northern districts.
Today, borewells and open wells irrigate more than half of the state's net irrigated area. Over-pumping groundwater lowers the water table, so conservation is urgent.
Micro-irrigation methods like drip irrigation deliver water drop by drop near plant roots, cutting evaporation and saving up to half the water used in flood irrigation.
Tamil Nadu's paddy calendar follows three main cropping seasons: Kuruvai, Samba and Thaladi.
Kuruvai is the short-duration summer crop sown around June when water is released from Mettur. Samba is the main long-duration crop grown through the Northeast Monsoon.
Thaladi is a second crop grown in the same field right after Kuruvai is harvested, helping delta farmers raise two harvests in a good water year.
Beyond paddy, millets like cholam, cumbu and ragi thrive in drier rain-fed districts because they need far less water and are rich in iron, calcium and fibre.
Pulses such as black gram and green gram are often grown in rice fallows. Their root nodules fix nitrogen, naturally restoring soil fertility for the next crop.
Commercial cash crops include sugarcane in river valleys, cotton in black-soil tracts, groundnut in sandy loam soils, and coconut along coastal and western belts.
In the Western Ghats and Nilgiri hills, cooler temperatures and well-drained slopes support plantation crops like tea, coffee, cardamom, pepper and nutmeg.
The Green Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s introduced high-yielding variety seeds, chemical fertilisers, and assured irrigation, lifting foodgrain production dramatically.

text.en: However, heavy chemical use can harden soil and pollute groundwater. Organic farming uses compost, green manure and bio-fertilisers to keep soil healthy for the long term.
Farmers also face market risks: when everyone harvests at the same time, prices can drop sharply. Regulated markets and Uzhavar Sandhais let farmers sell directly to buyers.
Minimum Support Price, crop insurance and low-interest cooperative bank loans protect families from losing everything when a cyclone or drought damages a harvest.
Allied activities like dairy farming, poultry, beekeeping and inland fisheries give rural households steady year-round income even during dry months.
In recent years, non-farm work in textiles, food processing and transport has grown alongside farming, reducing over-dependence on a single monsoon.
To judge any farming region, look at three clues together: water source, soil type and crop duration. Together they explain why delta plains grow paddy while dry uplands grow millets.
Sustainable agriculture in Tamil Nadu means combining traditional tank wisdom with drip irrigation, fair market access and soil-friendly farming for future generations.

problem.en: Why is the Cauvery delta called the rice bowl of Tamil Nadu, whereas drier western uplands grow more millets and groundnut?

text.en: Check the water and soil of the Cauvery delta.

why.en: Alluvial river silt is rich in nutrients, and canals from Mettur Dam plus Northeast Monsoon rains supply abundant standing water needed by paddy.

text.en: Compare this with rain-fed upland districts.

why.en: Upland soils drain faster and receive less canal water, so hardy crops like ragi, cholam and groundnut survive dry spells much better.

text.en: Connect crop choice to sustainability.

why.en: Matching crops to local soil and water avoids wasting groundwater and keeps yields reliable.

prompt.en: A friend says Tamil Nadu agriculture does not depend on rain. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: It depends on the monsoon and rivers.
